title: Serving through the body
hook: eating, working and resting can be worship

segments.voice: Yesterday, the rebbe, the Hasidic leader at the head of the table. Your line was a guide. Did you get a message off to someone who once showed you the way? Day one thousand one hundred ninety-four.

Where does worship happen? The easy answer is a building. A sanctuary, an ark, rows of seats, a quiet hour set apart from the rest of the week. And then there's everything else: the sandwich at your desk, the dishes, the shift at work, the nap on the couch. Two lists. Holy over here, ordinary over there. The Hasidic teachers looked at those two lists and refused to keep them apart. The sandwich, they said, can be worship too. Not instead of prayer, but alongside it. Today's word is the name for that refusal.
screen: `WHERE DOES WORSHIP HAPPEN?` → `HOLY HERE, ORDINARY THERE.` → `THE SANDWICH CAN BE WORSHIP TOO.`

segments.voice: Avodah b'gashmiyut. Avodah is service, worship, the same word once used for the service in the Temple. Gashmiyut is physicality, the stuff of the body and the material world. Service through the physical. First, the verse. Proverbs says, "In all thy ways acknowledge Him, and He will direct thy paths." Hasidic teachers leaned hard on the word all. Not only in the ways that look religious. In all of them. Second, the older roots. The Mishnah in Pirkei Avot teaches that all your deeds should be for the sake of Heaven. And the Talmud makes a bold comparison: while the Temple stood, the altar brought atonement, and now a person's table does. The kitchen table, set with food and with guests, takes up some of the altar's work. Third, the Hasidic turn. If God is present everywhere, then a meal eaten with a blessing before it and attention during it isn't a break from serving God. It's a way of serving. Working honestly, resting on the Sabbath, sleeping so you can rise and do good: all of it can be avodah, when it's done with the right intention. Fourth, the caution. This is not permission to call every appetite holy. The point isn't that whatever the body wants is worship. It's that the body, used with intention, can become a place where worship happens. Two lists become one.
screen: `SERVICE THROUGH THE PHYSICAL.` · `IN ALL THY WAYS.` · `A PERSON'S TABLE, LIKE AN ALTAR.` · `NOT EVERY APPETITE IS HOLY.` · then, large: `SERVE THROUGH THE BODY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: get ready to eat one meal as worship. Settle, and breathe. Think ahead to the next thing you'll eat today. See it in front of you. Before the first bite, you'll pause. If you say a blessing, you'll say it slowly, hearing each word. If you don't, you'll simply notice where the food came from, the ground, the rain, the hands that grew it and carried it and cooked it. Then you'll eat the first few bites without your phone, tasting them. For now, sit with that plan, and with the plain fact of your body breathing. The bell holds the time.
Avodah b'gashmiyut. Service through the physical: the Hasidic teaching that eating, working and resting, done with intention, can be worship. Today's word.
Your line: serve through the body. Today, eat one meal as worship: a pause before the first bite, and the first few bites with nothing in your other hand. Day one thousand one hundred ninety-four.

howItsDone: Observant Jews say a blessing before and after eating, and Hasidic teaching asks that ordinary acts like eating, working and sleeping be done with the intention of serving God.
